newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Bangladesh move closer to end water dispute.
newsitem.headline: India, Bangladesh move closer to end water dispute.

text.p: India and Bangladesh on Tuesday inched towards a solution to a decades-old water-sharing dispute, a major irritant in relations between the two countries, officials said.
Bangladesh Water Resources Minister Abdur Razzak and his Indian counterpart Janeshwar Mishra at official level talks identified the steps needed to forge a consensus on the issue.
"We have discussed in a friendly atmosphere and we have already identified our problems and we are very much close to solving them," Razzak told Reuters Television after the meeting.
"Surely we hope that it will be solved in future. We have come closer," he said.
The Ganges dispute has been a major irritant in relations between the two neighbours since India built its Farakka barrage near Bangladesh's northern border in 1974.
Dhaka says the barrage 18 km (11 miles) from Bangladesh's northern border obstructs the river flow and deprives the country of its fair share of water.

It says India diverts much of the water to meet its own requirements for irrigation and navigation during the dry season, while it releases excess water during the monsoon, causing extensive flooding in Bangladesh.
A statement by India's Water Resources Ministry quoted Mishra as saying that he hoped the initiative taken by the Indian government would lead to a mutually-acceptable solution.
Mishra said official-level discussions should continue to find a consensus on sharing of the waters.

Razzak on Tuesday had a luncheon meeting with Foreign Minister I.K. Gujral. He is due to meet Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Jyoti Basu, chief minister of West Bengal state, bordering Bangladesh, on Wednesday.
Basu is expected to visit Bangladesh in mid-November for further talks on water sharing.
Razzak stressed the need to find a long term solution to the issue before the onset of the next six-month dry season, which begins in December.
Bangladesh officials say more than 40 million people in northern and north-western Bangladesh are seeing their land gradually turning into desert because of the Farakka barrage.
Under the last agreement, which expired in 1988, Bangladesh received 34,500 cusec (cubic metres per second) of Ganges water during the dry season. Attempts to renew the agreement failed.
